meta.note: Ubiquitous-language ontology for task-framework's domain: the vocabulary the code embodies, and the explicit typed relations between terms (is-a, part-of, relates, persists, references, describes). Deliberately separate from concept_store/concepts.json -- that store is architecture PER MODULE (one summary per file, enforced 1:1 by tests/test_concepts.py) and answers 'what does this module promise'. This file is vocabulary PER DOMAIN TERM and answers 'what is this thing, and what is it to the others' -- a term here can span several modules, and a module can define several terms, so it does not fit concept_store's per-file shape. Ground truth is still the code; this is a durable, human-readable map of the graph rather than N separate summaries.

bounded_contexts.Task Tracking: The core domain: tasks (some flagged as epics), their checklists, the links between tasks, and which task is currently active.
bounded_contexts.Loop Memory: Durable takeaways the loop accumulates that nothing in Task Tracking or The Loop can hold: MemoryRecords and the closed vocabularies on them. Separate store, separate lifecycle, coupled to the rest only by a MemoryRecord's mandatory citation to the Task it was learned from.
bounded_contexts.The Loop: The four-pass methodology and everything it writes as it runs: the Methodology itself, its Grooming / Implementation / Introspection passes, the Risks a Grooming pass predicts, the GroomingGrade verdicts Introspection assigns, the GroomingAccuracy read across many Tasks, and the advisory Nudges the loop emits. These are recorded onto the Task, so the context is tightly coupled to Task Tracking by design -- it is the coupling, which is why it is named apart from Loop Memory rather than folded into it.
bounded_contexts.Architectural Knowledge: What each source module promises, tracked in concept_store/concepts.json -- describes the codebase itself, not tasks or memories.

Task.definition: One unit of work: id, epic flag, status, resolution (checklist), tags, notes, grooming findings, introspection reports. The single typed object the whole domain is built around. 'epic' is a plain boolean on this record (default False), not a subtype and not a term of its own -- a boolean carries everything the earlier two-value 'type' enum did, with no malformable value left to validate. Its sole effect is that an epic Task takes no parent; teams set it to mark a Task that others are grouped beneath, but that grouping is a convention, not a rule -- nothing requires a child's parent to be an epic. The parent/child hierarchy is a self-referential link from a Task to at most one parent Task, and no Task may be its own parent. A Task also carries a Scope naming the project it was created under, recorded at creation and never inferred afterwards.
Task.lifecycle: A Task is walked through four skills, each with one intention: task-create to open it, task-grooming to remove uncertainty before work starts, task-implementation to do the work, task-introspection to grade how well grooming predicted it and feed Loop Memory. None is mandatory, but skipping one leaves a Nudge behind.

Motivation.definition: The 'why' carried on a Task: the user or system consequence the work exists to produce, and what breaks if it is never done. Free prose rather than a value from any closed set, and deliberately apart from the ResolutionItem checklist that says what 'done' looks like and from the Grooming snapshot that says how to get there -- motivation is the field meant to still make sense to a reader long after the plan it justified has been forgotten. A Grooming pass is allowed to rewrite it in place: sharpening a thin motivation counts as repair, not annotation, and it is the one piece of a Task's original framing grooming is encouraged to change rather than only add to. When a Task exists because something surprised whoever opened it, that is recorded here at creation -- the earliest home for a Surprise, before any Introspection pass exists to hold one.

TaskStatus.definition: The lifecycle state carried on a Task, drawn from a fixed, closed set of four values (open, blocked, done, abandoned); its legal values and the legal transitions between them are the one state machine the domain enforces. 'done' and 'abandoned' are terminal.
TaskStatus.lifecycle: New tasks start 'open'. Non-terminal states may move to 'abandoned' directly; other transitions are checked against a table transcribed from the state model. Enforcement lives in exactly one place -- the lifecycle layer's status check and transition table -- never in a caller.

ResolutionItem.definition: One checklist entry (text, done) inside a Task's resolution list. A Task's progress is derived by counting these, never stored as a separate counter.

TaskEdge.definition: A directed, typed connection between two Tasks, with a relation drawn from a fixed, closed vocabulary. Stored separately from Tasks, never inside a Task's own record.

TaskStore.definition: The Repository for Task: reads and writes tasks, edges, and commits. Deliberately does no rule-checking of its own -- validation lives entirely in a separate layer.

ActiveTaskPointer.definition: Which task_id is currently 'active' for a given workspace -- a single in-memory value, not a stack, and not a field on Task itself. Keyed by working directory, so two repositories worked on at once each keep their own active task; nothing about it is persisted or survives a restart.
ActiveTaskPointer.lifecycle: A Scope names at most one Task active at a time: the Task whose pass through the Methodology is currently in hand. A Task becomes active when its pass begins -- when it is first framed, or when work is deliberately resumed on it later -- and stays active across the whole arc, through Grooming and Implementation. It is released when its Introspection is recorded: capturing the retrospective is itself what ends the Task's turn as active. Nothing else releases it -- reaching a terminal TaskStatus does not, because a finished-but-not-yet-introspected Task is exactly the one Introspection still needs named. Making a different Task active simply replaces the one that was; the active Task is surfaced once, when it becomes active, and not repeated. It is transient by form: it lives only in the moment, is no part of the Task's own record, and does not outlast the working session.

MemoryRecord.definition: A durable takeaway the loop exists to accumulate -- a constraint, a technique, or a recurring pitfall that Grooming's falsifiable predictions and Introspection's grades produced, and that nothing in Task Tracking can hold. doc 05 and CLAUDE.md call this a 'lesson'; there is no separate Lesson term because there is no separate thing -- a lesson's only persisted form is a MemoryRecord, so the two names would carry identical evidence and identical rules. Its 'standing' is a derived label, never a value it holds in its own right (see MemoryStanding); its citation to the Task it came from is mandatory, and its 'kind' is a closed vocabulary.

MemoryKind.definition: The kind of a MemoryRecord, drawn from a fixed, closed set of exactly three values (constraint, technique, pitfall). Doc 05 names 'constraint' and 'technique' outright; 'pitfall' earns its place from the accuracy signals, where a recurring 'wrong' or 'missed' grade is a lesson about the loop itself. The set is kept at three deliberately: a longer taxonomy is a decision to make on every capture.
MemoryKind.lifecycle: Set when the MemoryRecord is recorded (defaults to 'constraint') and validated in exactly one place -- the memory record path raises Rejected for any value outside the set. There is no transition machine; re-recording a slug may change its kind.

MemoryRelationship.definition: The label on one link joining a MemoryRecord to a Task, drawn from a fixed, closed set of exactly three values (learned_from, confirmed_by, contradicted_by). 'learned_from' is the mandatory citation every MemoryRecord carries; 'confirmed_by' and 'contradicted_by' are grades a later Task adds. A MemoryRecord's 'standing' is derived from how many confirming and contradicting links it has, never stored.
MemoryRelationship.lifecycle: Written when a MemoryRecord is recorded ('learned_from', implicitly) and when it is linked to a Task (any of the three, idempotently); validated in exactly one place -- the link path raises Rejected for a value outside the set. Links are never updated or deleted except by a forget, which cascades. Standing is recomputed from the surviving links on every read.

MemoryStanding.definition: How much a MemoryRecord can currently be trusted, expressed as one of five words (unverified, confirmed, contradicted, disputed, superseded). It is earned, not asserted: a lesson starts 'unverified' and gains or loses weight only as later Tasks re-encounter it and grade it confirmed or contradicted. Standing is always read off that track record rather than stored, so it can never disagree with the history it summarises -- the same reason the loop computes progress and grooming accuracy on read. 'unverified' is the honest default for a lesson nobody has tested again, stated plainly rather than dressed up as reliable. 'disputed' -- a lesson both confirmed and contradicted -- is surfaced rather than smoothed over, because a contradicted memory returned as though sound is an omission indistinguishable from an absence, and only the Task reading it can tell which side is right.

Concept.definition: A durable summary of what one source module promises and what must stay true of it -- description, contracts, invariants, evidence. Keyed by module path, enforced 1:1 against the real file tree.

SkillInvocation.definition: A record that a named skill (e.g. commit, task-grooming) ran, optionally against a Task. Deliberately just a lightweight log entry, not a stored, referentially-integral record -- the task reference is not validated. Exists for skill-usage observability only, scoped narrowly so it can't become a second home for decisions or notes.

Methodology.definition: The practice the whole framework exists to make cheap: the four-skill loop -- create, groom, implement, introspect -- together with the docs/methodology/ documents that specify it. It has no artifact of its own, only what each pass writes onto a Task and into Loop Memory. CLAUDE.md calls it 'the asset' and the storage/validation/serving code 'plumbing' subordinate to it: the ontology names every moving part (Grooming, Risk, Introspection, MemoryRecord) but this term names the thing they add up to. Its evidence is the first in this file to cite a docs/ file rather than a taskfw/*.py symbol, because the methodology is embodied in the skills and the methodology docs, not in code.

Grooming.definition: The pre-implementation pass that records a task's current best understanding as falsifiable risks/findings before work starts. Recorded as part of the Task and replaced wholesale each pass -- unlike Introspection, only the latest pass is kept, because grooming is a current-belief snapshot, not a history.

Risk.definition: One falsifiable prediction a Grooming pass makes about the work ahead -- a thing that might go wrong, or a claim that might not hold -- written so that Introspection can later say plainly whether it did. It is the one part of Grooming that is not thrown away and rewritten each pass: a Risk keeps its own identity, so a prediction Introspection has already graded is carried forward when the plan is re-groomed rather than lost because a later pass did not restate it. That surviving, graded Risk is the loop's primary evidence -- the falsifiable half of 'Grooming makes falsifiable claims, Introspection grades them'. Whether the machinery that carries a grade forward belongs behind a shared write path is an open question tracked as its own task, not a claim this ontology makes.

Introspection.definition: The post-implementation pass that grades how well Grooming's predictions held up and surfaces lessons for Loop Memory. Recorded as part of the Task as an appended series rather than Grooming's replace-in-place snapshot, since each report is evidence about one distinct execution and the series itself is the value.

Implementation.definition: The third pass of the Methodology: doing the work a groomed Task describes, once Grooming has removed enough uncertainty to begin. It is where the plan becomes a change, and where the outcome that Introspection later grades each Risk against is produced. Like Grooming and Introspection it has no artifact of its own, only what it writes onto the Task as it goes: Decisions logged when the choice is made, Commits, and ResolutionItems checked off as they land. Its one intention is to not reintroduce the uncertainty Grooming removed -- staying in scope, and recording reasoning as it happens rather than reconstructing it after.

Nudge.definition: A transient, advisory piece of text attached to the response of an action the caller already took, computed fresh each time. It never blocks the action or changes what gets stored, and it never hands back the content of a record the caller did not touch. What it points at is either context the caller already has (this task, this memory, this report), or a bare COUNT over records it names none of -- `loop_debt_nudge` tallies ungraded risks across the last finished tasks in the project on `tasks__set_active`. The aggregate is admissible because a tally is not a fact about any one of the records it counts; returning those records' text would be a push. It exists to keep an omission (nothing worth recording) from ever looking identical to an absence (nothing to record) -- collapsing that distinction into silence is the failure mode a nudge prevents.

IntrospectionNudge.definition: The Nudge that rides on the response to recording an Introspection report. It fires when the report carries a lesson but the Task has never cited a Loop Memory record -- the case where 'nothing here was worth promoting' would otherwise look identical to 'a lesson was dropped on the floor'. It points only at what the caller just wrote and the Task they wrote it against, never at a memory's content; whether a lesson generalises is the caller's judgement, not a bar this enforces, and a Task that has already promoted one lesson is not nudged again. It is the first concrete case the `Nudge` term names.

LoopDebtNudge.definition: The Nudge that rides on the response to `tasks__set_active`. Reports a bare COUNT -- how many of the last N finished Tasks in the project carried predicted Risks that were never graded -- over records it names none of, recomputed from `taskfw/accuracy.py:loop_debt` on every call so it can never disagree with what `tasks__grooming_accuracy` reports about the same Tasks. The aggregate is admissible for exactly the reason the `Nudge` term gives: a tally is not a fact about any one of the records it counts, so returning it is not a push. Fires only when the count is non-zero; a clean loop is silent, not a zero report. Companion to `task_debt_nudge`, which rides on the same call but speaks about the one Task just made active rather than the loop across recent ones.

TaskContext.definition: The whole pull-based working bundle assembled for one Task in a single call -- its identity, decisions, grooming, graph of neighbours, commits, related tasks, and matching loop-memory lessons, in one fixed order, built fresh every time. Some sections are exact lookups where a wrong answer would mislead; two -- related tasks and lessons -- are approximate matches and the first to go when the bundle outgrows its size budget. Every shortfall is reported, and by a route specific enough that a caller can always tell a section trimmed for space from one that was genuinely empty -- collapsing that distinction into silence is the one thing a pull interface cannot afford. This is the concrete shape of 'context is pulled, never pushed': nothing about a Task reaches an agent on its own, only through this bundle, and only because the agent asked.

Commit.definition: A record that a specific commit (sha, repo) was made against a Task. Stored apart from Task itself, keyed by (task_id, sha), with an idempotent insert -- recording the same sha against the same task twice is a no-op, not an error. Same shape as TaskEdge: never addressed by an id of its own, only reachable through the task it was recorded against.

Event.definition: One entry on a Task's append-only activity log: a timestamped piece of text carrying a kind label from a fixed, closed vocabulary (TASK_EVENT_KINDS: note, decision, status, hooks_event), enforced in the lifecycle layer the same way every other closed vocabulary in the domain is -- no caller can write a kind another caller could not. A Decision is one kind of Event; a status change is another. Not a distinct class per kind -- the kind label is the only thing that tells two Events apart -- and the log is never addressed by an id of its own, only read back through the Task it belongs to.

Decision.definition: One kind of Event recorded against a Task: the design-reasoning entry, set down at the moment a real choice was made. What makes an Event a Decision is only its kind label -- the value 'decision' from the closed TASK_EVENT_KINDS set -- on an otherwise uniform log entry; there is no separate decisions store to hold it.

GroomingAccuracy.definition: The Methodology's feedback edge read in aggregate: how well a Grooming pass's Risks predicted, gathered across many finished Tasks instead of one. Introspection grades each Risk against a single Task; GroomingAccuracy is what those grades amount to once collected -- the loop's report on itself. Computed from the graded Risks on every read.

GroomingGrade.definition: The verdict Introspection passes on a single predicted Risk, graded against what the Implementation pass actually did: did predicting this help -- did it come true with its mitigation ready, or force the change that avoided it -- or was the pass spent on noise. A label carried on the Risk, the way MemoryKind is a label on a MemoryRecord, absent until Introspection assigns it. Its vocabulary (GROOMING_GRADES: materialized, avoided, wrong) is closed for COUNTING but not enforced on write -- Introspection may record a grade outside the set, and GroomingAccuracy buckets that as `unrecognised` and still reports it rather than dropping it. This is a deliberate difference from TaskStatus or MemoryKind, where an off-vocabulary value is refused: a grade is an observation worth keeping, not a state that corrupts a machine. A Surprise that no Risk predicted is deliberately not a GroomingGrade (see the `Surprise` term): with no prediction beneath it there is nothing for a verdict to be about. One GroomingGrade is Introspection closing the Methodology's feedback edge for a single prediction; GroomingAccuracy is what those verdicts amount to across many finished Tasks.
GroomingGrade.lifecycle: Assigned by a single Introspection pass, after Implementation, and carried by its Risk from then on. Re-grooming the same Task keeps the verdict rather than discarding it, so a judgement Introspection has already made is never lost.

GroomingGradePredictiveValue.definition: The one-line answer to 'are Grooming's predictions earning their keep' -- the share of graded Risks whose prediction paid off, whether by coming true with its mitigation ready or by forcing the change that avoided it. A Risk graded as noise is the only kind that counts against it. It is deliberately absent, not zero, when nothing has been graded yet: 'no evidence' is a different statement from 'everything predicted was wrong', kept distinct the same way an empty Scope is not a project. It is a headline for a human reader, never a control input -- the loop's own 'grooming is asking the wrong questions' signal is derived separately and does not read this figure, so how it is rounded or whether it is shown at all changes what a caller sees but never what the loop acts on.

Surprise.definition: A finding an Introspection pass records that no Risk predicted -- 'a surprise no prediction anticipated', in the words of the introspection methodology. It is the negative space of the feedback edge: a GroomingGrade is a verdict on a prediction that was made, a Surprise is what remains when there was none, which is why it is deliberately kept out of the closed grade vocabulary -- with no prediction beneath it there is nothing for a verdict to be about. It carries its own free text rather than a label from a set, and has no identity or store of its own: it lives inside the Introspection report and travels with it. It is the missed item itself, not the lesson it might become -- promotion into Loop Memory is a separate, deliberate step, and most surprises are never promoted. Repeated Surprises are a signal in their own right: grooming is not asking enough questions.

Scope.definition: Which project a record belongs to: a scheme-prefixed string derived from the working directory, never typed by hand. `git:<host>/<path>` when a git origin was readable, `path:<abs>` when there was none, `hint:<raw>` when a caller supplied a repo string that could not be resolved to a directory. An attribute, not an entity -- it has no identity of its own, only equality, which is the single operation every consumer needs. The prefix is part of the value because it records HOW the project was known: a fallback must never compare equal to a derived answer, or an omission becomes indistinguishable from an absence. The empty string is a fourth, distinct case meaning 'project unknown' -- carried by every Task written before the field existed, never backfilled, and treated as compatible with every scope rather than as a project of its own.
Scope.lifecycle: Derived once, at record creation, from the workspace in hand, and never recomputed on read -- a record does not change project because someone later read it from somewhere else.

relations.subject: Motivation
relations.note: The free-text 'why' field on the Task record, written at creation by tasks__create and editable afterwards by tasks__update. Unlike TaskStatus or Scope it is drawn from no closed vocabulary and carries no lifecycle enforcement -- there is no malformable value for a caller to reject, so no rule needs a home. It is also the one part of a Task's original framing a Grooming pass may rewrite in place (docs/methodology/03-grooming.md: fixing a thin motivation is 'repair, not annotation'), even though Grooming otherwise only replaces its own snapshot and leaves the rest of the Task alone.

relations.subject: TaskStatus
relations.note: The state field on the Task record. Its closed vocabulary (TASK_STATUSES) and its legal transitions are enforced only in the lifecycle layer, so no caller can validate status differently from another.

relations.subject: ResolutionItem
relations.note: Nested inside task.resolution. Cardinality: zero or more -- resolution defaults to an empty list and nothing enforces a minimum, matching the framework's 'nothing is required' stance.

relations.subject: TaskEdge
relations.note: A TaskEdge only exists in relation to two Tasks; it is never addressed by an id of its own, and removing one is deliberately ungated so a legacy relation type can't get stuck. The parent/child hierarchy is deliberately NOT a TaskEdge -- it is the self-referential Task.parent field, and 'parent_of' was left out of TASK_EDGE_RELATIONS so the hierarchy has exactly one home. Its only rules: an epic Task takes no parent (lifecycle.check_parent), and no Task is its own parent (lifecycle.check_save).

relations.subject: TaskStore
relations.note: The Repository for the Task aggregate; persistence and validation stay separable because TaskStore enforces no rules itself.

relations.subject: ActiveTaskPointer
relations.note: Names the currently-active task_id keyed by working directory (`mcp_server._scope`); never a property stored on Task itself. Deliberately NOT keyed by the Scope term, despite that function's name: a `git:` scope collapses two worktrees of one repo onto one project, which is the right answer for 'which project owns this task' and the wrong one for 'which task is open in this window'.

relations.subject: MemoryRecord
relations.note: Cited to the task it was learned from -- a pointer into Task Tracking from a different bounded context, never reachable by walking Task's own fields. The citation is one MemoryRelationship row ('learned_from'); see that term for the other two.

relations.subject: MemoryKind
relations.note: The kind label on the MemoryRecord. Closed vocabulary (MEMORY_KINDS) of three values, validated only in the memory record path -- the same single-enforcement-home rule TaskStatus follows.

relations.subject: MemoryRelationship
relations.note: The closed label (MEMORY_RELATIONSHIPS, three values) on each MemoryRecord-to-Task link; those links are what 'MemoryRecord references Task' is built from, and the counts of the 'confirmed_by' / 'contradicted_by' links are what MemoryStanding is computed from on every read. Validated only in the memory link path.

relations.subject: MemoryStanding
relations.note: The trust label on the MemoryRecord, parallel to 'MemoryKind part-of MemoryRecord' and 'TaskStatus part-of Task' -- but where those are fields a caller sets, this one is nothing a caller can set: it is only ever what the record's history with later Tasks adds up to, kept derived so it cannot drift from that history.

relations.subject: MemoryStanding
relations.note: Standing is a reading of how later Tasks have graded the lesson -- confirmed when it held again, contradicted when it did not -- mirroring 'GroomingAccuracy references Risk': which records it reads, not what it stores. Same derive-don't-store reason as progress-from-checklist: a stored judgement can drift from the evidence it claims to summarise.

relations.subject: Concept
relations.note: SourceModule is deliberately NOT a defined term -- it is a placeholder for 'some file in the repo', declared as the one allowed non-term relation object (NON_TERM_OBJECTS in tests/test_ontology.py) rather than given a definition, because a source file is not a domain noun. Keyed by module path, not by task_id -- Architectural Knowledge shares no term with Task Tracking or Loop Memory; the only connection between the three bounded contexts is this ontology file itself.

relations.subject: SkillInvocation
relations.note: Carries an optional reference, but it is unvalidated and one-directional -- a Task has no field or list that points back to the skills invoked against it.

relations.subject: Methodology
relations.note: One Task is walked through the loop; the Methodology's only footprint is what each pass writes onto the Task (grooming, introspection, decisions, commits) and into Loop Memory (lessons). 'describes' rather than 'part-of' because the practice is the larger thing and the Task is what it operates on -- the Task exists without ever being groomed, the loop does not exist without a Task to run against.

relations.subject: Grooming
relations.note: The falsifiable-claims half of the one feedback edge that separates this from a paperwork ritual (CLAUDE.md: 'Grooming makes falsifiable claims. Introspection grades them.'). Grooming is also 'part-of Task' -- the pass belongs to the Methodology, its recorded output belongs to the Task.

relations.subject: Introspection
relations.note: The grading half of the feedback edge, and the step CLAUDE.md names as the first to rot because skipping it always feels like progress. Like Grooming it is also 'part-of Task': the pass is the Methodology's, the appended report series is the Task's.

relations.subject: Implementation
relations.note: The pass between Grooming and Introspection -- create, groom, implement, introspect -- and the only one that changes the codebase. It owns no store of its own: its outputs are Decisions, Commits, and checked ResolutionItems on the Task, exactly as Grooming's output is the Task's grooming and Introspection's is the report series. Named as its own term so GroomingGrade can be defined as a verdict on what this pass did, rather than leaving 'implement' an unnamed step inside Methodology's definition.

relations.subject: Introspection
relations.note: Introspection grades every Risk against what Implementation actually did; a GroomingGrade is that comparison for one prediction. Before Implementation was a term the feedback edge had a verdict (Introspection), a thing predicted (Risk) and an aggregate (GroomingAccuracy), but no name for the reality the prediction was about.

relations.subject: Grooming
relations.note: Recorded as part of the Task and replaced wholesale each groom pass -- except its Risks, which merge by id (see 'Risk part-of Grooming').

relations.subject: Risk
relations.note: The one exception to Grooming's wholesale-replace rule: risks merge by id across re-groom passes so a graded verdict is never silently lost, while every other Grooming field still replaces in place.

relations.subject: Introspection
relations.note: Recorded as part of the Task; an appended series rather than Grooming's replace-in-place snapshot, reflecting that each pass is a distinct piece of evidence.

relations.subject: MemoryRecord
relations.note: Introspection is where a lesson is surfaced for possible promotion into Loop Memory -- a report carrying a lesson with no cited memory triggers a Nudge, so the omission stays visible instead of silent.

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: One bundle is assembled per task_id on demand and has exactly one Task as its subject -- 'describes' rather than 'references' because that Task is what the whole bundle is about (the neighbour Tasks it also embeds are the separate 'references Task' edge).

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: The bundle's graph section pulls a Task's edges fresh on every call, capped per direction -- edges are read into the bundle, never duplicated into it.

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: The bundle's lessons section is the guaranteed read path back into Loop Memory (see MemoryRecord's Introspection link for the write side) -- without it, a lesson only reached an agent if it happened to look for it directly. Like related, this section is an approximate (bm25) match and among the first trimmed when the bundle is over budget, with any drop reported in `truncated` -- so the exact/approximate split is visible from both approximate sections' relations, not only from 'references Task'.

relations.subject: Nudge
relations.note: A nudge either speaks about the one task or memory the triggering call already touched (`task_debt_nudge`, `stale_memory_nudge`, `finish_nudge`, `introspection_nudge`) or reports a bare count over records it does not name (`loop_debt_nudge`, over recent finished tasks in the project). Never the content of a record the caller didn't ask about -- it rides on a response, it does not fetch a fact for the caller to read.

relations.subject: Nudge
relations.note: One nudge checks whether a just-recorded Introspection report's lessons have been promoted to a MemoryRecord yet, without itself writing to Loop Memory.

relations.subject: IntrospectionNudge
relations.note: `Nudge` names a mechanism -- advisory text attached to a response -- and on its own stays close to the code symbol it cites. `IntrospectionNudge` is domain vocabulary because the compound binds that mechanism to the `Introspection` term: it names a standing fact about the loop -- 'an introspection pass produced a lesson that never reached Loop Memory, and the loop says so' -- not an implementation detail. It is not sugar over `Nudge`; it is the edge that connects `Nudge` to `Introspection`, which is why it carries its own `references Introspection` relation. Same triple form as `Decision is-a Event`, but what earns it an entry is the association with another term, not merely being one instance of the parent.

relations.subject: IntrospectionNudge
relations.note: Reads the report just appended by `tasks__add_introspection` (`task.introspection[-1]`) for lesson-shaped entries, and the Task's `memory_links` for an existing `learned_from` citation. Points back at both -- context the caller already pulled -- and writes to neither; promotion to a MemoryRecord stays a separate, explicit `task_memory__record` call.

relations.subject: LoopDebtNudge
relations.note: Vocabulary for the same reason as `IntrospectionNudge`: the compound binds the nudge mechanism to a domain concept -- the loop reporting its own debt, the count of finished Tasks whose predicted Risks were never graded. Its anchor is the ungraded-`GroomingGrade` aggregate rather than a single term, which is also why it is the one nudge that returns a bare count instead of pointing at a record the caller touched -- the exception `Nudge`'s definition calls out now has a term to hang off instead of only a clause.

relations.subject: LoopDebtNudge
relations.note: Counts finished Tasks whose predicted Risks have no GroomingGrade -- the ungraded-risk tally comes straight from `taskfw/accuracy.py:loop_debt`, the same source `tasks__grooming_accuracy` reads, so the nudge's number and the accuracy report's number are recomputed from one place and cannot drift apart. It names none of the counted Tasks; the count is all that crosses back.

relations.subject: Commit
relations.note: A Commit only exists in relation to the task it was recorded against, keyed by (task_id, sha) with an idempotent insert -- same shape as TaskEdge, never addressed by an id of its own.

relations.subject: Decision
relations.note: Logged via the same generic Event path status changes use, distinguished only by its 'decision' kind label.

relations.subject: Decision
relations.note: A Decision is an Event with its kind label set to 'decision'; a status change is the same Event mechanism with a different label. The Decision term and this relation describe that entry from two angles: what a decision-kind Event is for (the Decision term) and that it is one value of the closed TASK_EVENT_KINDS vocabulary on a uniform log (this relation).

relations.subject: Event
relations.note: An Event only exists on one Task's append-only log; it is never addressed by an id of its own, only read back through the Task -- the same shape as TaskEdge and Commit. The closed TASK_EVENT_KINDS vocabulary is what tells a Decision-kind Event from a status-change Event.

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: The bundle's commits section pulls a Task's recorded commits fresh on every call, matching TaskContext's own definition -- without this relation the definition named a section the ontology did not otherwise back with a term.

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: The bundle's decisions section pulls a Task's decision-kind events fresh on every call, matching TaskContext's own definition -- without this relation the definition named a section the ontology did not otherwise back with a term.

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: Distinct from 'describes': the bundle also embeds full Task summaries beyond the one it was built for, by two unlike paths. Parent and children arrive in the graph section as an exact deterministic traversal (store.get(parent), children WHERE parent=?) -- a wrong answer there would be misleading, not merely unhelpful. Full-text neighbours arrive in the related section as an approximate bm25 match, and related is the first section trimmed when the bundle is over budget. Neither path ever returns the same Task the bundle describes.

relations.subject: GroomingAccuracy
relations.note: The per-Risk 'graded' verdicts across finished tasks are the sole source; the grooming_accuracy tally in an introspection report is recomputed from them every call and only cross-checked, never read back as truth. Same derive-don't-store reason as progress-from-checklist and standing-from-links -- a stored aggregate can drift from its own evidence.

relations.subject: GroomingAccuracy
relations.note: The aggregate form of the one feedback edge (CLAUDE.md: 'Grooming makes falsifiable claims. Introspection grades them.'). Risk carries that edge for a single task; GroomingAccuracy closes it for the loop itself -- repeated 'wrong' grades mean grooming asks the wrong questions, repeated 'missed' grades mean it asks too few, and both are signals to change grooming rather than note the miss.

relations.subject: GroomingGrade
relations.note: The verdict label on a Risk's 'graded' field, from the closed GROOMING_GRADES set (materialized, avoided, wrong); absent until Introspection assigns it and merged forward by risk id across re-grooming passes so a graded verdict is never silently lost. Closed for counting only -- an unrecognised grade is reported as `unrecognised`, never refused on write.

relations.subject: GroomingAccuracy
relations.note: GroomingGrade is the unit GroomingAccuracy counts: its tallies, predictive_value, and the 'wrong'-share signal are all counts of GroomingGrade values across finished Tasks, where the sibling 'references Risk' edge is about which Risks it reads rather than what it tallies. A value outside GROOMING_GRADES is bucketed as 'unrecognised' and still reported, never dropped, so the grade count can never silently disagree with the risks seen.

relations.subject: GroomingGradePredictiveValue
relations.note: One field of the GroomingAccuracy result, computed on the same read from the same graded-Risk counts. It is their one-line summary and nothing more -- a caller that distrusts it can ignore it and re-derive its own from the counts sitting beside it, which is why it is carried as a convenience rather than a stored number that could fall out of step with them.

relations.subject: GroomingGradePredictiveValue
relations.note: Built from GroomingGrade values only -- the grades that count as useful over every recognised grade in the window. A grade outside the closed set is reported elsewhere but left out of both halves of this ratio, so a stray value can never pull the figure around; it describes exactly the grades Introspection assigned from the set and no others.

relations.subject: Scope
relations.note: The project field on the Task record, written once at creation by tasks__create. Empty on every Task predating the field, which reads as 'project unknown' rather than as a project.

relations.subject: Scope
relations.note: task_commits.repo is normalised through the same derivation, so a commit's project and a task's project are the same kind of value and can be compared. This column is where free-text project identity was observed fragmenting into five spellings of two projects.

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: The bundle's two approximate sections read Scope, and diverge on it: `related` excludes a neighbour from another project outright, while `lessons` returns it marked cross_project, because loop memory exists to generalise across projects and hiding a foreign lesson would defeat the subsystem to enforce a boundary it was built to cross. The bundle's task section also carries Scope verbatim plus a files_root resolved from it (scope.local_root), so a reader can turn the task's relative files into real paths instead of guessing the project root; files_root is null, never a guess, when the root is not knowable from the reading workspace.

relations.subject: Surprise
relations.note: A free-text entry in the Introspection report's `missed_surprises` list (legacy reports: `surprises[].lesson`), appended with the report and never addressed on its own. The same shape as `GroomingGrade part-of Risk`, one level up: a GroomingGrade hangs off the Risk it grades, a Surprise hangs off the whole report because it is precisely the item that has no Risk to hang off.

relations.subject: Surprise
relations.note: The deliberate contrast, made an explicit edge rather than left only as prose inside GroomingGrade's definition. A GroomingGrade is a verdict on a Risk's prediction; a Surprise is what remains when there was no prediction, so `missed` is held out of the closed GROOMING_GRADES set (the comment on it in taskfw/risk.py says so) and lands in the report's `missed_surprises` field instead. Same feedback edge, opposite side: repeated wrong grades mean grooming asks the wrong questions, repeated surprises mean it asks too few.

relations.subject: GroomingAccuracy
relations.note: The negative-space unit GroomingAccuracy counts, sibling to `references GroomingGrade`: surprises are tallied per finished task, and a high share of them across groomed tasks becomes the loop's 'grooming is not asking enough questions' signal. Surprises from tasks that were never groomed are counted apart and kept out of that ratio -- an ungroomed task has no prediction it could have missed, so folding it in would push the number toward 100% for a reason the signal does not mean.
